  1   I. INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q.     Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.    My name is Orland Whitney. I am employed by the New Mexico Public Regulation

 4         Commission ("NMPRC" or "Commission") as a Staff Engineer in the Utility Division. My

 5         business address is P.O. Box 1269, Santa Fe, New Mexico 87504.




 6   Q.    Please summarize your education and professional experience.

 7   A.    I graduated from New Mexico State University with a Bachelor of Science degree in

 8         Electrical Engineering in August 2022. I was concurrently enrolled in the Master’s

 9         Accelerated Program at New Mexico State University and graduated with a master’s

10         degree in December 2023. I have been employed as a Staff Engineer with the NMPRC

11         since September 2023. My work includes review of electric utility filings involving

12         engineering, service quality, location approvals, renewable energy, interconnection-related

13         matters, grid modernization, line-extension and service-territory issues, reliability

14         reporting, and other technical utility matters.




15   Q.    From what perspective are you testifying in this proceeding?

16   A.    My testimony addresses electrical-engineering and utility-engineering issues, including

17         resource capacity function, line losses, voltage-level factors, used-and-useful support, Rule

18         440 traceability, transmission and distribution plant, local generation plant, AMS

19         deployment, legacy-meter replacement, line-extension policy, and large-load facility

11   Q.    What is El Paso Electric Company requesting in this proceeding?

12   A.    El Paso Electric Company ("EPE" or "Company") requests approval of revised New

13         Mexico retail electric rates pursuant to Advice Notice No. 317. In its Amended

14         Application, EPE states that the filing uses a twelve-month Base Period ending September

15         30, 2025, and a Historical Test Year Period adjusted under Rule 530. EPE seeks recovery

16         of a non-fuel base-rate revenue deficiency of approximately $70.7 million, offset by a

17         $0.241 million reduction in miscellaneous service revenue, for a net revenue increase of

18         approximately $70.5 million. The exact amended Schedule A-01 amounts are $70,723,779

19         for the base-rate revenue deficiency and $70,482,824 for the net revenue increase. EPE

20         states that the requested increase is driven in material part by capital additions since its

 7                Metering System (AMS) deployment and legacy-meter replacement, including equipment

 9                traceability; (5) used-and-useful engineering considerations for transmission, distribution,

10                and local generation plant; (6) replacement and retirement facts relevant to, but distinct

11                from, depreciation accounting; (7) EPE’s proposed line-extension and large-load

12                protections, including facility sizing, customer-specific cost responsibility, and payment or

13                security obligations when requested load does not materialize, decreases, or terminates

14                early; and (8) limited electric-service and unit-identification issues concerning the Palo

15                Verde Nuclear Generating Station.

11         technical inputs are tied to legitimate utility functions; whether they are in service and used

  1   V. LINE LOSS AND VOLTAGE-LEVEL FACTORS
 2   Q.           Why do line loss factors differ between transmission and distribution customers?

 3   A.           Line losses come from resistance in the wires. The power lost as heat equals current squared

 4                times resistance (I²R). Because the current is squared, doubling the current quadruples the

 5                loss. The reason current is squared is that two things grow together: more current means

 6                more electrons bumping into the wire, and each electron is moving faster, so each collision

 7                is harder. Both effects multiply, which is what the squaring captures. At lower voltages,

 8                more current is needed to deliver the same power, so losses grow sharply as voltage drops.

 9

10                Transmission customers are further upstream, and they take power at high voltage and

11                bypass the lower-voltage facilities where most losses occur. Distribution customers, served

12                at primary or secondary voltage, sit further downstream and bear those losses. So,

13                transmission customers impose fewer losses per delivered kWh than primary or secondary

14                distribution customers, and that difference drives the voltage-level adjustment factors used

15                in the cost-of-service and rate-design studies.6

18                attaches the 2021 Analysis of System Losses prepared by Management Applications

19                Consulting, Inc., dated September 2022. The study states that the results develop

20                cumulative expansion factors for both demand and energy losses by discrete voltage levels

 5   VI. ADVANCED METERING SYSTEM AND LEGACY METERS
 6   Q.    Why are AMS and legacy-meter issues included in your testimony?

 7   A.    AMS deployment and legacy-meter replacement have engineering implications for

 8         functionality, communications coverage, and service continuity. Staff’s accounting and

 9         revenue-requirement witnesses address the corresponding cost-recovery treatment.

10   Q.    What did EPE state regarding AMS approval, functionality, and deployment?

11   A.    EPE witness Novela states that the AMS Project was approved in Docket No. 21-00269-

13         granular consumption data, enable two-way communication, and include remote turn-on

14         and turn-off capability. The project includes a communications network, a head-end

15         system, and a meter data management system. Novela reports that implementation was
